title: Active and passive pieces
outcomes: Counts the squares a piece can reach to judge how active it is
Finds the worst-placed piece and improves it
Places a rook behind a passed pawn rather than in front

steps.text:
A piece is worth what it can do: the squares it can reach and what it attacks. Count them. Before starting something new, find your worst-placed piece and improve it.
**Rule of thumb:** once your minor pieces and queen are out, clear the back rank so your rooks protect each other (connect them).

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on c1 is boxed in.

line.say: The pawn steps aside to open a diagonal.

claims.statement: The bishop on c1 has no legal move.

steps.caption: The same bishop on b2 has a long diagonal.

claims.statement: The bishop on b2 has eight squares.

steps.text: Count the squares, then ask what the piece can do from them. A knight on the rim (the edge of the board) has few squares. A rook is most active with open files to enter (files with no pawns on them), and **behind a passed pawn** (a pawn with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its own or a neighbouring file), its own or the enemy's, rather than in front of it. In the next two positions only the rook's place differs.

steps.title: Same rook, behind or in front
steps.prompt: Only White's rook differs between the two positions. In which one can White win? Predict first, then check.
Before you counted squares: which of your own pieces would you have called the worst placed in the last position, and did the count agree?
